newsitem.title: CHINA: WTO chief sees China becoming "pillar" of trade.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief sees China becoming "pillar" of trade.

text.p: Negotiations on China's entry to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) have entered their final phase and Beijing must become a pillar of the world trade system, WTO Director General Renato Ruggiero said.

Addressing a symposium on the service trade in Shanghai on Saturday, the second day of a six-day visit to China, Ruggiero said the WTO increasingly needed China to become an active member, the Xinhua news agency said in an overnight report.

Ruggiero, due on Sunday in Beijing for meetings this week with Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi as well as President Jiang Zemin and Premier Li Peng, was expected to try to find ways to accelerate China's admission and stress to China's leaders the advantages of membership, diplomats said.

"China must become one of the pillars of the world trade system," Xinhua quoted Ruggiero as saying, and he added that the world's most populous nation was already an important member of a global economy marked by mutual dependence.
Negotiations on China's admission to the WTO had entered their final phase, Ruggiero said.
China's entry as soon as possible would inject new vigour into a multilateral global trade system, he said.
The WTO increasingly needed China as an active member to ensure the organisation was a real global trade system able to shoulder responsibilities seen for the 21st century, he was quoted as saying.
Numerous issues remain to be resolved on China's decade-long entry application to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor organisation, the WTO, diplomats say.

They say they have seen little shift in China's position in recent months and cite a need for Beijing to lift a wide range of barriers including opening its agriculture markets, financial services, trading rights and distribution systems as well as clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry.

Ruggiero would use his visit to listen to the concerns and objectives of China's leaders and to explain the positions of other countries taking part in the bilateral negotiations that decide a country's entry, his spokesman said.
Diplomats from countries involved in the bilateral talks with China said Ruggiero faced a tough task.

China's chief negotiator, Vice Foreign Trade Minister Long Yongtu, told the symposium Beijing would unswervingly persist with entry talks, adding that it would take time for China and the world to coordinate and adjust to each other.

Areas where China has yet to meet demands from Europe, Japan and the United States include trading rights -- allowing foreign firms to engage in imports and exports in China -- and national treatment on distribution.

Other China monopolies that unite developed nations and many others in negotiations with Beijing are financial services -- prising open the insurance and banking sectors -- as well as accounting, law firms, education and tourism and travel.
The Cairns Group of major agricultural exporting countries, including Australia, Argentina, Canada and New Zealand, was concerned about access to China's agricultural markets.

However, agreement has been reached on the principle that China will be allowed to enter under a phased system accorded to developing nations that would give it time to introduce reforms over a certain period.
